title: How to parameterise an equivalent-circuit empirical battery model from time-domain data
author: Blyth, Gupta, et al.
materials: Experimental data are collected using the Galvanostatic intermittent titration technique. Galvanostatic means current is controlled and voltage is measured; intermittent titrations mean the electrochemical reaction is run (a titration is performed) for short periods (intermittently). Intermittent current pulses show both the instantaneous and transient changes in cell voltage. These can then be used to identify the various model parameters. Intermittent pulses keep temperature changes to a minimum, which reduces error in the parameter estimates. Steps are as follows.
using the previously found interpolants voc(SOC) and R0(SOC).

steps.title: Set up cell and cycler
steps.instruction: Secure the cell in a low‑resistance test rig with independent current‑carrying and voltage‑sense cables, connect it to a battery cycler that controls current, monitors safety, and records current and voltage, and provide thermal control (e.g., climate chamber or surface cooling) while continuously monitoring cell temperature.

steps.title: Define experimental hyperparameters
steps.instruction: Set the following hyperparameters: test temperature Ttest = 25 °C; pulse current Ipulse = 1.8 A; pulse duration tpulse = 180 s; settle time tsettle = 2 h; number of RC pairs n = 2; τ1min = 5 s, τ1max = 5 s; τ2min = 180 s, τ2max = 180 s; ΔtR0 window (not applicable, N/A).

steps.title: Run pulse‑charge/discharge experiment
steps.instruction: Collect galvanostatic intermittent titration data by alternating current pulses and rests at the desired test temperature.

substeps.instruction: Set cell temperature to 25 °C.
Charge cell to 100 % state‑of‑charge using manufacturer‑recommended procedure.
Set cell to the test temperature Ttest.
Pause for a rest period tpause.
Discharge at current Ipulse for time tpulse.
Repeat discharge‑pulse and pause sequence until the lower voltage cutoff is reached.
Pause for tpause.
Repeat charge‑pulse and pause sequence until the upper voltage cutoff is reached.

steps.title: Determine nominal cell capacity
steps.instruction: Find the greatest achieved capacity throughput from the pulse‑test data and define it as the nominal capacity Qnom.

substeps.instruction: Take the experimental data from the pulse‑test (or a pseudo‑open‑circuit voltage sweep if available).
Select the dataset recorded at the hottest Ttest and the lowest Ipulse.
Apply Coulomb counting (integrate current) to obtain capacity throughput Q(t) at each time point.
Set Qnom = max[Q(t)], the maximum capacity throughput observed.

steps.title: Calculate capacity throughput Q(t)
steps.instruction: Compute Q(t) in amp‑hours using the trapezium rule: dQ/dt = I(t) × 3600, or Q(t)=∫₀ᵗ I(τ) × 3600 dτ, with Q(0)=0.

steps.title: Compute state‑of‑charge (SOC)
steps.instruction: Obtain SOC as a function of time by scaling the capacity throughput with the nominal capacity.

substeps.instruction: Take the experimental data from step 3.
Use Qnom from step 3.
Apply Coulomb counting: dSOC/dt = I(t) × 3600 / Qnom, or SOC(t)=∫₀ᵗ I(τ) × 3600 / Qnom dτ, with SOC(0)=1.

steps.title: Measure and record open‑circuit voltage
steps.instruction: Extract the relaxed voltage at the end of each pulse‑relaxation cycle and pair it with the corresponding SOC.

substeps.instruction: For each pulse‑cycle, take the final voltage measurement after the cell has rested (most relaxed state).
Record the pair (SOC, Voc) for that discharge pulse.
Repeat for all discharge pulses, then for all charge pulses.
Repeat the whole procedure for each tested cell temperature.
Use the collected (SOC, Voc, T) samples to build separate interpolation functions Voc(SOC,T) for discharge and charge.

steps.title: Fit series resistance R0 and fast transient (R1, τ1)
steps.instruction: Identify R0 (and optionally R1, τ1) by fitting a 1‑RC model to the initial part of each current pulse.

substeps.instruction: Set up the cell model (Eq. 1) using the Voc(SOC) interpolant and a single RC pair.
Select a single current pulse and extract the data segment where I ≠ 0.
Define the fitting window from pulse start time t₀ to t₀ + Δt (Δt is the R0‑window).
Choose initial guesses for R0, R1 and τ1 (use previous pulse parameters if available; otherwise use domain knowledge or the midpoint (τ1min+τ1max)/2 for τ1).
Fit R0, R1 and τ1 to the voltage data v(t) in the window, assuming they are constant, by numerically integrating Eq. 1 and minimizing ‖vmodel(t;R0,R1,τ1) − v(t)‖² subject to τ1min ≤ τ1 ≤ τ1max.
Record the fitted R0 together with the SOC at t₀ and the test temperature Ttest as a tuple (R0, SOC(t₀), Ttest).
Discard the fitted R1 and τ1 values.
Repeat the procedure for every discharge and charge pulse, and for each tested temperature, to obtain R0 samples over SOC and T.
Assemble separate interpolants R0(SOC,T,I) for discharge and charge.

steps.title: Fit remaining RC parameters (Ri, τi)
steps.instruction: Identify the RC resistances and timescales for each pulse using the previously obtained Voc(SOC) and R0(SOC) interpolants.

substeps.instruction: Set up the cell model (Eq. 1) with Voc(SOC) and R0(SOC) interpolants.
Select a single pulse and extract the data where I ≠ 0.

Fit each RC pair (Ri, τi) (i = 1…n, with n from hyperparameters) to the voltage data by assuming Ri and τi are constant during the pulse and minimizing the least‑squares error, subject to τimin ≤ τi ≤ τimax.
Compute the average SOC across the pulse (average of SOC at pulse start and end) and denote it SOC̄.
Record the sample (Ri, τi, SOC̄, Ttest).
Repeat for all discharge and charge pulses, and for each temperature and pulse current.
Collect separate datasets for discharge and charge.

steps.title: Build final interpolations for all parameters
steps.instruction: Create functional representations of each identified parameter over state‑of‑charge, temperature (and current if needed) using appropriate interpolation methods.

substeps.instruction: For Voc(SOC,T) use a monotonic interpolator (e.g., linear or PCHIP) because open‑circuit voltage increases monotonically with SOC.

For R0(SOC,T,I) and each Ri(SOC,T,I) and τi(SOC,T,I) test three approaches: curve‑fitting, standard interpolation, and monotonic interpolation; prefer monotonic methods to avoid overshoot (negative resistance).
If noisy data are present, consider smoothing splines; otherwise linear monotonic interpolation is sufficient.
Prevent extrapolation beyond the measured SOC‑T‑I domain; optionally add fictitious points (e.g., SOC = 1.01) to allow the solver to handle slight overshoots safely.
Validate each interpolant on a hold‑out dataset before using it in simulations.
